title: What Sellers Should Know About Closing Costs
content_html:
When you sell a home, the number you see on your listing price isn't the number you'll actually walk away with. Between the purchase price and your final proceeds sits a set of expenses commonly called "closing costs." Understanding what these are, who typically pays for what, and where there's room to negotiate can help you plan realistically and avoid surprises at the closing table.

What Are Closing Costs, Exactly?

Closing costs are the fees and expenses associated with finalizing a real estate transaction, separate from the sale price itself. For sellers, these are usually subtracted from the proceeds at closing, so you receive your net amount after everything is settled rather than paying out of pocket along the way. Some of these costs are fixed by law or by the terms of your existing loan; others are negotiable between buyer and seller as part of the purchase agreement.

Common Costs Sellers Typically Cover

While every transaction is different and specific terms are negotiated in the purchase contract, sellers in California commonly encounter some combination of the following:

  • Real estate commissions. Historically the largest single line item for most sellers, commissions are negotiated directly between a seller and their listing agent and are not set by law or by any fixed industry standard. Because rates vary by agreement, this is a conversation to have directly with your agent early in the listing process.
  • Title and escrow fees. Escrow acts as the neutral third party that holds funds and documents until all conditions of the sale are met. Title fees cover the cost of insuring clear ownership. Who pays which portion of these fees is often a matter of local custom and is negotiable in the contract.
  • County transfer tax. California allows counties and some cities to charge a tax on the transfer of real property. The specific rate and who is responsible for it (buyer, seller, or split) is often addressed in the purchase agreement, and rates can vary by jurisdiction, so it's worth confirming the applicable amount for your specific property with escrow or title.
  • Outstanding loan payoff. If you have a mortgage, HELOC, or other lien on the property, the remaining balance — plus any accrued interest through the closing date — is paid off from your proceeds before you receive the remainder.
  • Prorated property taxes. Property taxes are typically prorated between buyer and seller based on the closing date, so you're only responsible for the portion of the tax year you actually owned the home.
  • HOA-related fees. If your home is in a community with a homeowners association, you may be responsible for transfer fees, document preparation fees, or a prorated share of dues, depending on the HOA's own rules and the terms you negotiate with the buyer.
  • Repairs or credits negotiated after inspection. It's common for buyers to request repairs or a credit toward closing costs after a home inspection reveals issues. Whether and how much you agree to is part of the negotiation, not an automatic cost.
  • Recording fees and miscellaneous document fees. Smaller administrative fees for recording the deed and other paperwork with the county are typically part of closing costs as well.

What's Negotiable — and What Isn't

Some closing costs, like paying off your existing loan balance, aren't negotiable — that debt exists regardless of who's buying. But many other costs are genuinely open to negotiation between buyer and seller, including who pays transfer taxes, how title and escrow fees are split, and whether the seller offers any credit toward the buyer's own closing costs as an incentive. These terms are typically worked out as part of the offer and counteroffer process, which is one reason it helps to have a clear strategy going into negotiations.

Disclosure Obligations Can Affect Costs, Too

California law requires sellers to disclose known material facts about a property's condition to prospective buyers. These disclosures aren't a "cost" in the same sense as a fee, but they can influence negotiations around repairs, credits, or price adjustments once a buyer reviews them. Understanding your disclosure obligations before you list can help you anticipate where negotiation is likely to happen.

How to Estimate Your Net Proceeds

Before listing, most sellers find it useful to work through a rough "net sheet" — a simple worksheet that starts with an estimated sale price and subtracts anticipated costs (loan payoff, commission, title/escrow fees, prorated taxes, and any anticipated repair credits) to arrive at an estimated net. Because commission rates, transfer tax responsibility, and other line items are all negotiable or property-specific, this is best done with input from your agent and escrow officer rather than estimated from memory or a generic online calculator. Timing your sale can also affect your bottom line in less direct ways, since seasonal market patterns can influence pricing and negotiating leverage.

Preparing Ahead Reduces Surprises

Many closing-cost surprises come from unresolved liens, unexpected HOA fees, or repair negotiations that could have been anticipated with earlier preparation. Addressing known issues, gathering HOA documents in advance, and getting a clear payoff statement from your lender early in the process all help you go into escrow with a more accurate picture of your expected proceeds.

Working With an Agent on Closing Cost Questions

Because so many of these costs are negotiable, property-specific, or dependent on the details of your loan and HOA, a conversation with your listing agent and escrow officer early in the process is the most reliable way to get an accurate picture for your specific sale. George Khazanovskiy, a Temecula Valley real estate agent, is available to answer questions about the listing process for sellers in the area.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do sellers always pay the real estate commission?

Commission arrangements are negotiated directly between a seller and their listing agent and can vary from one transaction to another. There is no fixed or legally mandated rate, so this is a conversation to have directly with your agent.

Can closing costs be paid from the sale proceeds instead of out of pocket?

Yes — in most transactions, closing costs are deducted from the seller's proceeds at closing rather than paid separately, so you receive your net amount after all costs are settled.

Are property taxes included in seller closing costs?

Property taxes are typically prorated between buyer and seller based on the closing date, meaning you're responsible only for the portion of the tax year during which you owned the home.
